analysis.one_liner: Phases out tariffs on most goods traded with South Korea and opens government purchasing to Korean firms.
analysis.headline: The Senate never voted on this bill; instead Congress passed the House companion on October 12, 2011, and the Korea trade agreement took effect in March 2012.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would approve and implement the US-Korea Free Trade Agreement, phasing out tariffs on most goods crossing between the two countries over a schedule of years. It includes origin rules, customs enforcement, and safeguard procedures letting injured US industries petition for temporary import relief, plus special protections for textiles and light trucks. It opens US government procurement to Korean firms and allows foreign investors to arbitrate claims against the United States. Revenue offsets come from higher customs fees, front-loaded corporate tax payments, and small tax-enforcement changes.
analysis.who_benefits: US exporters — especially farmers and ranchers selling beef and pork into Korea — gain market access. Korean automakers gain duty-free access to the US market. Consumers benefit from tariffs coming off many goods. US light-truck makers keep a 25% tariff on Korean trucks for seven years before it phases out.

how_it_helps.text: Phases out tariffs on originating goods: Korean passenger cars drop from the 2.5% rate to duty-free by year 5, while Korean light trucks keep a 25% tariff through year 7 and phase down to free by year 9-10.
Opens US government procurement to products and services of Korea by amending the Trade Agreements Act of 1979.

Creates safeguard procedures: unions, firms, and trade associations can petition the International Trade Commission for relief from surging Korean imports, with relief of up to three years, plus special motor-vehicle and textile safeguard tracks.

Adds customs enforcement — recordkeeping, penalty-free correction of origin claims, and verification and suspension powers for textile and apparel imports — to police that only qualifying goods get the tariff break.

Pays for the tariff cuts with offsets: the customs merchandise processing fee rises from 0.21% to 0.3464% for December 2015 through June 2021, and corporations with $1 billion or more in assets must front-load estimated tax payments in 2012 and 2016.

analysis.who_pays: Workers in import-competing industries face tougher competition from Korean goods; taxpayers stand behind investor-state arbitration claims against the United States; importers and consumers pay a higher customs processing fee for five and a half years; and large corporations must front-load tax payments to cover the bill's revenue cost.

drawbacks.text: Safeguard relief is limited: import relief lasts at most three years including extensions, textile relief at most four, and no relief is available ten years after the agreement takes effect.

The bill authorizes the United States to resolve investor claims through investor-state dispute settlement under the agreement's arbitration procedures, letting foreign investors pursue claims against the US outside the ordinary courts.

The offsets shift costs elsewhere: the merchandise processing fee on imports rises by more than 60% for 2015-2021, and $1 billion-plus corporations must front-load estimated tax payments — a timing shift, not a permanent tax cut for them.
The 25% truck tariff stays for seven years, which protects US light-truck makers at the expense of buyers of trucks.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Tariff elimination lowers prices for consumers and opens Korea's market to US exporters, especially in agriculture, and the safeguard, customs, and textile provisions give import-sensitive industries some protection. But the gains and losses are uneven: critics of the deal, including the Economic Policy Institute, projected the agreement would cost the US economy on the order of 159,000 jobs over its first five years, concentrated in manufacturing, while a large share of the gains flows to multinational firms and to importers. The investor-state arbitration provision exposes taxpayers to claims brought outside the normal court system. On balance the deal leans toward concentrated interests, with safeguards narrower than the exposure.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate never voted on this bill; it sat on the calendar while Congress instead passed the House companion measure, and President Obama signed the trade agreement into law in October 2011.

narrative.text: Introduced October 3, 2011 by Senator Baucus for himself, Senator Hatch, and Senator McConnell, and read twice and referred to the Finance Committee.
The Finance Committee ordered the bill reported favorably without amendment on October 11, 2011, and it was placed on the Senate calendar under General Orders the same day.
The Senate never took a floor vote on the bill; its last recorded action was a written committee report filed September 20, 2012.

The agreement instead became law through the House companion bill, which passed both chambers on October 12, 2011 — the Senate approving it 83-9 — and was signed by President Obama on October 21, 2011; the agreement took effect on March 15, 2012.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Supporters of the trade deal got what they wanted without this bill ever reaching a vote: the tariff cuts, procurement access, and investor arbitration took effect, while opponents' warnings of manufacturing job losses went unheeded.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The deal's supporters — it became law anyway

sides.party_line_note: The Senate bill's sponsorship was bipartisan — one Democrat and two Republicans — but when the companion bill came up, nearly all Republicans in both chambers voted yes while most House Democrats voted no; the Senate passed it 83-9.

industries.note: The bill phases the 2.5% US passenger-car tariff to zero by year 5 and lets producers average regional value content by model line, easing qualification for duty-free treatment. Cheaper Korean imports increase competition for US auto plants and workers, while car buyers benefit from lower prices.

Korean trucks keep a 25% tariff through year 7 of the agreement before phasing to free — protection the bill locks in for the industry that makes US pickups. It shields those producers at the expense of truck buyers.

By approving the agreement, the bill opens Korea's market to US farm exports under phased Korean tariff cuts. Farmers and ranchers gain customers; the benefit comes from the other country's tariff cuts rather than from a cost to US consumers.

The bill writes in yarn-forward-style origin rules, a 7% weight tolerance, verification and suspension powers over Korean textile shipments, and a four-year textile safeguard. It gives the industry both enforcement tools and a temporary import-surge valve.

Importers get duty-free treatment on qualifying Korean goods but also pay a higher merchandise processing fee — 0.3464% versus 0.21% — from December 2015 through June 2021. Lower tariffs lower shelf prices; the fee increase trims that gain slightly.

Section 106 authorizes the United States to resolve covered claims through the agreement's investor-state dispute settlement procedures, giving foreign investors a standing channel to challenge US measures outside the courts. Taxpayers stand behind any awards.

These corporations must front-load estimated tax payments — 0.25% more in the third quarter of 2012 and 2.75% more in the third quarter of 2016 — to offset the bill's revenue cost. It is a timing shift rather than a permanent tax change.
